name: Zane Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior crime reporter at the regional daily, mostly for the website. My day starts at seven checking the overnight police statements, then I'll write up whatever happened, a crash on the bypass, a burglary spree, a stabbing outside a club. Afternoons I'm usually at court or out at a scene, knocking on doors. Evenings I sometimes wait outside court for a verdict.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being out, talking to families, getting the real story behind the police line. What wears me out is checking. I got a defendant's age wrong in my first year and Neil, the news editor, still reminds me. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy transcripts, but I check everything twice now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds sensible. Most of the fuss dies down eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like every new gadget, useful but overhyped. I'd say it to the lads at work and my dad. Hard work still matters more than any program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job looks safe in this one. Nobody is going to send an AI to stand outside the court at six in the evening waiting for a jury to come back. Crime is the one beat the paper always keeps, because it gets the most readers. I'm still learning, but there's a place for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going and get better at checking facts. I'd keep putting about five hundred a month into savings. I'd go to the police press office's monthly briefing and build more contacts there. And I'd keep using the transcript tool when it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. My job's safe and I've got savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your cushion.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine months of pay saved, and I own a small flat that my dad helped me buy. He runs a car repair garage across town, has done for thirty years. So if things ever went badly, I'd have family to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just getting things right. One more mistake like the age one and Neil would stop trusting me. That's the pressure I feel, not machines.

say: I'd say AI is like every gadget: **useful but overhyped**.
I'd say **hard work** still matters more than any program.
think: Privately my job looks **safe**, since no AI waits outside court for a verdict.
**Crime** is the beat the paper always keeps because it gets readers.
do: Get better at **checking facts** after his early mistake.
Attend the police **press briefing** monthly to build contacts.
feel: **Calm**: his job feels safe and he has **savings**.
S0.quote: Nobody is going to send an AI to stand outside the court at six in the evening waiting for a jury to come back.
fieldNote: He believes **crime coverage** is the paper's safest beat.
His father's **garage** is a family safety net in the background.

steps.text: Double-check every fact and name before filing crime stories
Save five hundred a month alongside his flat payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one hits closer to my mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should adapt, not complain. Some jobs change, that's how it's always been. My grandfather fixed horse carts before cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my morning is turning police press releases into stories, and that's exactly the part of my job a computer would take first. The paper would keep the senior crime reporter and maybe drop me. I'd be lying if I said I wasn't worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools once the senior lads were using them, because I'd rather be useful than proud. I'd push to do more court and door-knocking, the parts a computer can't. I'd keep saving. And I'd talk to my dad about the garage, not to join, just to know the door's open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not scared. I've got options most people my age don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should adapt, not complain. Are you adapting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. I'm not the first to jump, I want to see it work. But I'd get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a mate who lost his job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get back out there, find something, ask your family. I wouldn't tell him to wait for government money. That's how my dad raised me.

He'd advise **work and family** over government help.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools after senior crime reporters adopt them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after their own and get ready, not wait for the government. Families have to help each other. I'd say that at work and at Friday prayers with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job goes. It's thinking work, so it's 2028. My dad has been telling me for ten years there's always a job for me at the garage, and in this picture I'd finally take him up on it. Repairs are hands-on, so that's three more years, and the garage's paperwork would go even sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at the garage part-time straight away, evenings and weekends, learning the work. I'd put some of my savings into the garage, maybe for electric car diagnostic kit. I'd keep the flat. When the paper cut me, I'd go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I didn't go to university to fix cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your dad say when you told him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say, finally. Then he'd put me under a car the same afternoon. He doesn't do sympathy, he does work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. Maybe we'd buy the robots. Maybe the garage turns into a place that owns machines instead of fixing them. That's for later.

I'd say it at work and at **Friday prayers** with my dad.
think: Privately my job goes in **2028**, because it's thinking work.
I'd finally take up my dad's offer at the **garage**.

Hands-on repairs give him **three more years**, which he spots clearly.
He'd **invest** in the family firm rather than wait for help.

steps.text: Work evenings and weekends at his dad's car repair garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit easier to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get a trade, so people should get one. Apprenticeships, not degrees. I'd say that to my younger cousins especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to learn to fix electric cars properly, and people will need their cars fixed long after they stop needing me to write about crime. AGI writes the crime stories by 2031. The robots come for repairs around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the paper and learn the AI tools, so I'm useful there for a few years. I'd start an evening course in electric vehicle repair. I'd help my dad modernise the garage. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I was doing something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the garage busy enough for two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy enough that my dad turns work away. He's 58 and his back's going. In five years he'd want me there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, especially the court stuff. But I'd rather be useful than nostalgic.

I'd tell my cousins to choose **apprenticeships**, not degrees.
think: Privately learning to fix **electric cars** outlasts writing about crime.

do: Learn the **AI tools** at the paper to stay useful.
Start an evening course in **electric vehicle repair**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to learn to fix electric cars properly, and people will need their cars fixed long after they stop needing me to write about crime.
fieldNote: He'd build a **second skill** while staying in journalism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time to prepare, so nobody should panic. Do your job well and learn something useful on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the ten years to be a good crime reporter first, because I'd hate to leave a job I never got good at. My job looks safe for most of that. Then around 2032 I'd move toward the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the paper and get properly good. I'd learn the AI tools as they come in. I'd keep saving and maybe put some money into the garage. And I'd learn basic repairs on weekends, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does getting properly good look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting the first call from the police press office, not the third. Having families trust me with their story. Neil not checking my copy twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the garage, and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's family, and family is the one thing I'd trust in all five pictures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to learn a trade properly. What would help is good apprenticeships for people my age, and help for family businesses like my dad's to buy new equipment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me were raised to believe. Hard work used to be the safe bet, and I'm not sure what the safe bet is when a machine never gets tired.

He owns a **small flat**, has nine months saved, and his dad runs a car repair garage.
He goes from **calm** to alarmed if AGI comes in two years, then settles with more time.
His answers lean on **family and trade**, with the garage as his long-term plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time to learn a trade properly.
